news.title: Will 30-Year US Treasury Yields Climb Higher? | Goldman Sachs
news.summary:
Summary:
- Goldman Sachs analyst Muhammad Qubbaj expects US long-term Treasuries to remain under pressure due to elevated energy prices and subdued demand from institutional buyers. The 30-year yield around 5.7% is the highest since 2002.
- In the near term, energy prices (driven by Middle East tensions) are the key driver of longer-duration rates, with supply from heavy government issuance adding to volatility.
- The Fed’s path is influencing long-end yields: while front-end rates may rise, the Fed signaled less “policing” of the long end, meaning the 30-year yield must find its own level attractive to pensions and insurers.
- Global factors are pushing yields higher in Germany and Japan as well, tied to higher policy paths, higher risk premia for long bonds, and debt absorption concerns.
- The U.S. debt-to-GDP trajectory is not seen as an unsustainable spiral; deficits around 6–7% of GDP with ~6% nominal growth imply a gradual drift rather than an explosive move.
- The market is not pricing in a high likelihood of a 30-year rally; 30-year yields of 5.5%+ are considered historically cheap in real terms, but a clear catalyst is absent amid heavy supply and uncertain inflation.
- Potential downside for yields exists if nominal growth remains around 5% and the economy absorbs new issuance, but a move toward 4.25% on the 30-year would require a recession or a major growth shock, which is not currently anticipated.

news.title: Lower US Treasury yield view persists despite biggest quarterly surge since 1994: Reuters poll | 99.9 Radio USA
news.summary:
US long-term treasury bond yields outlook (as of early Oct 2026)

- The Reuters poll suggests US 10-year yields are expected to ease over the coming months, with a median forecast of about 5.00% by year-end, 4.90% in six months, and 4.75% in a year.
- Despite the biggest quarterly surge since 1994, strategists remain broadly bearish on sustained high yields, arguing the market may have overestimated near-term Fed tightening and that policy might loosen later.
- Key pressure factors include persistent inflation dynamics, expectations of additional Fed rate hikes (priced in by futures), and heavy government debt issuance plus funding needs from AI-related tech spenders.
- Some strategists see fair value in the 4.50%–5.00% range for the longer end, assuming less aggressive future Fed tightening.
- The survey notes a repeated pattern of underestimating the 10-year yield’s rise this year and highlights a regime shift where long-end rates reflect tighter financial conditions even without aggressive policy action.
- Two-year yields are expected to fall to about 4.70% in three months, 4.60% in six months, and 4.25% in a year, according to the poll.
- Analysts emphasize the ongoing influence of term premium and the market’s response to macro data, suggesting yields may stay elevated if inflation remains persistent or if the Fed signals tighter policy.

Key takeaway: The consensus view is for modestly lower long-term yields from current levels over the next year, but the outlook remains uncertain and sensitive to inflation, Fed policy signals, and debt issuance dynamics.

news.title: US 10-Year Yield Steadies as Fed Outlook Mulled
news.summary:
US long-term Treasury bond yields outlook (based on the article)

- US 10-year yield held near 5.3% after retreat, amid hawkish Fed minutes suggesting potential further hikes by year-end.
- Fed outlook: All 19 policymakers supported September rate hike; most projected another increase by year-end. Market pricing implies a ~78% chance of a December hike; likelihood of no change this month.
- Supporting factors: Elevated inflation risks, robust growth, wide budget deficits, and high corporate debt keep long-duration yields near multi-year highs. Oil-market tensions and Middle East supply concerns add to inflation risk.
- Recent dynamics: 10-year yields briefly rose to about 5.32% (near levels last seen in 2002) before easing; strong 10-year note auction and shifting oil prices influenced moves.
- Market expectations: >80% of rate futures pricing for at least one additional rate hike this year; investors awaiting weekly jobless claims for labor-market clues. 30-year yields also hit multi-decade highs around 5.70% amid similar thematic pressures.

Bottom line: The near-term path for long-term Treasuries remains upward-biased given hawkish Fed expectations, persistent inflation risks, and supportive but volatile macro factors like oil prices and fiscal/debt dynamics.

news.title: U.S. Treasury yield outlook points lower despite market surge
news.summary:
US long-term treasury bond yields outlook analysis:

- Despite a sharp year-to-date rise in the 10-year yield (up ~120 bps and near 5.34%), bond strategists expect closer-to-term declines in long-end yields over the coming months. 
- A Reuters poll of about 60 fixed-income strategists projects the 10-year yield to ease to 5.00% by year-end, then 4.90% in six months and 4.75% in a year.
- The view contrasts with market pricing of additional Fed rate hikes: rate futures imply at least three more hikes, while futures imply the 2-year yield falling to about 4.70% in three months, 4.60% in six months, and 4.25% in a year.
- The disconnect arises from expectations that inflation may cool or that policymakers will tighten less than priced in, keeping long-term rates on a downward path despite near-term volatility.
- Context note: rising yields have been influenced by global inflation fears and risk premia linked to geopolitical tensions; mortgage-backed securities dynamics (negative convexity and hedging flows) can amplify near-term moves but may fade as refinancing incentives decline.

Bottom line: For long-term Treasuries, analysts anticipate eventual easing in yields over the next year, even as the market currently prices in further Fed tightening and strong inflation risk in the near term.

news.title: Lower US Treasury yield view persists despite biggest quarterly surge since 1994: Reuters poll | KELO-AM
news.summary:
US Treasury bond yields: Reuters poll (early Oct) suggests a continued view that yields will ease over coming months, despite the 10-year yield posting its largest quarterly rise since 1994/2002 highs. Key points:

- Median forecast: 10-year yield at about 5.00% by year-end, 4.90% in six months, and 4.75% in a year (based on a poll of ~60 fixed income strategists).
- Rationale for lower yields: belief that Fed hikes may be less aggressive than priced in, and that markets have overreacted to rate-hike expectations; models suggest fair value closer to 4.50–5.00%.
- Near-term dynamics: futures imply at least three more Fed hikes in coming months; two-year yields expected to fall modestly (to ~4.70% in three months, 4.60% in six, 4.25% in a year).
- Risks to view: a subset of forecasters expect the 10-year to stay higher than current forecasts in the near term; the longer-term trend remains uncertain.
- Supporting context: heavy borrowing by tech firms for AI and increased Treasury issuance add to yield pressure; recent US growth surprised to the upside (Q2 GDP +2.2% annualized); term premium and the Fed’s policy path are central to the regime shift in rates.
- Takeaway: despite the recent surge, many strategists hold a view for lower yields ahead, though conviction is wavering and the path hinges on the Fed's actual tightening stance and financial conditions.

news.title: U.S. Treasury yield outlook points lower despite market surge
news.summary:
U.S. Treasury bond yields outlook analysis:

- Despite a sharp year-to-date rise in yields (the 10-year around 5.34% at times, up ~120 bps), bond strategists expect yields to ease over the coming months.
- Reuters poll of nearly 60 fixed-income strategists (Oct 5–7) projects the 10-year yield at:
  - 5.00% by year-end
  - 4.90% in six months
  - 4.75% in one year
- The sell-off has been driven by persistent inflation concerns and higher global rates, with markets also pricing in further Fed hikes.
- The two-year yield is forecast to fall more firmly: to about 4.70% in three months, 4.60% in six months, and 4.25% in a year, even as futures imply at least three additional Fed increases.
- Some strategists, like Schwab’s Collin Martin, argue fair value may lie in a 4.50%–5.00% range for the 10-year, suggesting current levels may be somewhat overstated unless the Fed tightens more aggressively than anticipated.
- Mechanics such as agency MBS hedging can amplify near-term yield moves due to negative convexity and forced selling to manage interest-rate risk, though this impact can diminish as refinancing slows.

Bottom line: The prevailing view among strategists is a downward yield trajectory over the medium term, even as the near term remains volatile and rate hike expectations keep yields elevated in the short run.

  2) StoneX TV 업데이트는 중국 제조업 PMI가 50 상회, 구리 정광 타이트(파업 이슈·TC 하락) 등으로 “조심스러운 개선” 가능성을 언급하지만, 동시에 중국 내 구리 재고 증가와 니켈 구조적 과잉을 지적합니다. 즉 단기 수요·재고 신호가 혼재되어 있어 당장 매수 역추세 진입을 정당화할 만큼 강한 추세 전환 팩트는 아닙니다. 기계적 청산 신호를 뒤집을 근거로 보기 어렵습니다.
- 보조 참고: 일목은 구름 안·양운(상승 구름)이지만 이는 보조입니다. 규칙상 매도 판단을 바꾸지 않으며, 재진입 시에는 초기 비중을 보수적으로 시작하는 정도의 리스크 관리만 고려하겠습니다.

실행
- 보유 중이라면 청산. 이후 Donchian 상단(20일 또는 100일) 상향 돌파가 나올 때만 재진입하며, 신규 진입 시 트레일링 스탑(최근 고점 − 3×ATR)을 재설정합니다.

news.title: The LME Weekly Review: 28 September - 2 October 2026
news.summary:
Summary:

The LME Weekly Review (28 Sept–2 Oct 2026) signals a generally softer base-metals backdrop amid macro headwinds. Key points relevant to a price outlook and macro context for copper, aluminum, and zinc:

- Broad metal weakness: Aluminum (-5.1%), zinc (-4.8%), copper (-2.5%), lead (-4.0%), nickel (-4.3%), tin (-0.6%). Energy costs and higher yields/dollar strength weighed on sentiment; China’s Golden Week added uncertainty.
- Copper outlook: Prices pressured by macro factors and positioning, despite some supply-side support from tighter visible stock. Copper cash–3s narrowed vs prior week but remain sensitive to energy costs and financing conditions. The market needs physical demand signals (post-holiday buying, warehouse draws) to confirm sustainability; copper must hold around the $14,000/t level to avoid renewed selling pressure.
- Aluminum outlook: The weakest among the trio, down 5.1% to $3,100.50/t, with prices slipping intrawweek even as LME stocks remained relatively tight. The combination of macro weakness and positioning dominated, suggesting limited near-term upside unless energy costs ease or physical demand improves.
- Zinc outlook: Down 4.8% to $3,710.50/t, with price declines coinciding with weaker SHFE/open interest. Zinc faces a challenging near-term path absent stronger demand signals, though Chinese exports could offer some relief. Cash-3s eased somewhat, but any renewed warrant cancellations or stock draws could spur further downside.

Macro backdrop driving metal prices:
- Oil and rates: Oil rally and US 10-year yields around 5.2% supported inflation concerns early in the week; relief later as Gulf exports recovered and US–Iran talks tempered supply fears. European diesel-stock releases offered some relief, but China’s export stance for October added supply uncertainty.
- Energy costs: Lower energy prices would aid production/freight costs, aiding metals; however, financing conditions remained restrictive unless energy/financial conditions relax.
- China: Official manufacturing PMI just above 50.0 (50.1), with credit/housing support measures but unclear fuel for broad demand recovery. Holiday period (1–7 Oct) means the next test is whether physical demand and warehouse draws resume post-holiday.

Bottom line:
- Near-term risk remains skewed to the downside for copper and zinc on macro headwinds and tighter financing, with aluminum most vulnerable due to persistent weak sentiment despite tightening physical signals. A sustained rebound would require firmer fundamental demand signals in China post-holiday and clearer improvement in energy/financing conditions. Copper would particularly need price support around the $14,000/t level to avert renewed selling pressure.
